item.content:encoded:
The San Francisco Giants are going into a rebuild after trading away several top names at the MLB Trade Deadline, such as Luis Arraez, Heliot Ramos, and Robbie Ray. But with every rebuild, there's always a possibility for a familiar face to get a second chance with the franchise, depending on specific needs.
It's clear the Giants bullpen is one of those specific needs, holding a bullpen ERA of 4.18 and only collecting 30 saves this season. With many young pitchers looking to pave their path into the bullpen, this club needs a veteran reliever that it can rely on.
Across the league, the Pittsburgh Pirates announced Tuesday afternoon that they've designated former San Francisco Giants closer Camilo Doval for assignment as a corresponding move to activate Kirby Yates off the injured list.
Isn't that crazy how the world of baseball works? Doval spent his best years as a member of the Giants organization, holding a 3.29 ERA in 275 games for the franchise from 2021 to 2025, when he was traded to the New York Yankees. As a Giant, Doval collected 107 saves. Elsewhere, between the Yankees and the Pirates, Doval has recorded two saves.
Should the Giants Reunite with Doval?
This season, Doval holds a 4.30 ERA and a 1.52 WHIP with New York and Pittsburgh, having pitched well with the Pirates, but not well enough for the team to keep him around. Pirates manager Don Kelly had a blunt statement about Doval that the Giants know well.
“He had some really good games and a couple tough ones,” Kelly said via Aiden Stepansky of MLB.com. “He's got some really good stuff, and ultimately, it really just came down to being able to maximize innings.
It's not like Doval has lost all of what made him an All-Star in 2023, but he hasn't been that pitcher since. However, having tested the waters away from San Francisco, and then the Giants testing the waters without Doval, perhaps it's a reunion that has to happen.
Doval seemed to have figured it out the first month he was in Pittsburgh, pitching to a 2.84 ERA in August. But in September, it's been a different story, in which he's posted a 5.68 ERA in 6.1 innings across seven games.
Bringing Doval back to a franchise where he has previously felt comfortable and confident could be beneficial. As a veteran closer, he has the opportunity to mentor the younger players, while learning from them as well. San Francisco might be making the right choice by following the path that seems laid out before them.
According to MLB's DFA rules, within seven days of the transaction, the player can either be traded or placed on outright or unconditional release waivers. So, the Giants could be a team to watch for the next few days to see if they're a fit for their former reliever again.
Dominic Minchella is a 2024 Eastern Michigan University graduate with a BA in Communications, Media, and Theatre Arts and a Journalism minor. He covers Major League Baseball for On SI and spends his free time watching games and sharing his insights.

item.content:encoded:
September 22, 2026
The Phillies gave Saturday away, then gave themselves a golden chance to take it back.
But in almost textbook Philadelphia Phillies fashion, they let it go.
Brooks Raley loaded the bases in relief of Andrew Painter one out into the bottom of the sixth, and with a one-run lead, then gave up a Brett Baty liner into center that a diving Justin Crawford could only trap between his glove and the grass for another Mets run scored – and with the bases still full.
Interim manager Don Mattingly yanked Raley as soon as he could for Chase Shugart, and he walked in another to Ronny Mauricio – a .173 hitter at the bottom of the New York order – before a warning-track flyout from Francisco Lindor mercifully ended the frame.
The Phillies set themselves up with a bases-loaded answer of their own in the top of the seventh, after Trea Turner and Alec Bohm drew walks and Luis Arráez singled around a Kyle Schwarber groundout and a Bryce Harper strikeout. But under the pressure situation, Bryson Stott hacked a roller through the grass to second and was left slamming his helmet into the dirt as the Mets jogged back to their dugout without any damage.
The night unraveled from there. The Phillies lost to the Mets, 10-3, up in Queens. Orion Kerkering got tagged for the second straight game, letting up four more runs in the eighth, then was demoted to Triple-A after in a move that essentially exiles the struggling reliever from the roster.
They came back with a 7-2 win the next day, behind a stellar outing from ace Cristopher Sánchez that salvaged a 2-2 split in a four-game series, but with the whole weekend taken into account, it wasn't any kind of silver lining.
The Phillies are supposed to be a playoff team, and still more than likely will be, but they had four games against a Mets club living in the NL East basement right there for the taking. It was the schedule's last gimme. And yet they couldn't help but throw two of those games down the gutter, for little other reason than that they couldn't get out of their own way.
The Phillies were supposed to, or at least wanted fans to think, that they turned over a new leaf at the plate, hitting through August with the kind of small ball approach that their power-heavy lineup went out of its way to avoid for way too long, but they've since reverted back to the old habits and stubborn cold streaks that have long overstayed their welcome.
And the Phillies were supposed to have, or rather praying for, a somewhat stable bullpen after the trade deadline, but now it's so fickle and with so little time left that decisions seem destined to come down to "what starter moves into the bullpen for the postseason?"
It's been this way for five years now, through many big-money contracts that feel like they're never quite living up to the price tag, through many more failed looks at bargain-bin arms, two (and what's looking on track to be three) managerial changes, a dramatic infield shuffle mid-season, and increasingly suspect prospect development that begs an increasingly scarier question of what kind of long-term future does this club really have?
The Phillies aren't a serious baseball team. Not anymore, at least.
They're still good, sure, in the sense that they can – and again, more than likely will – qualify for a spot in October.
But really, they could've locked that spot up a week ago.
Instead, they're 8-10 through September. They punted any possible shot at the NL East title out the window once they let the Braves go 4-3 against them across their final two series, and left a Diamondbacks club that has notoriously broken their hearts before with a faint (and therefore dangerous) glimmer of hope in the final NL Wild Card chase, while leaving a best-of-three road playoff series in Atlanta as the expected prize.
And oh yeah, they do still have to play two good teams that can easily exhaust and bury them before the Phils can even think about any of what might come after.
So where really is the contender in all of this?
Certainly the Phillies are going to lean on their elite starters between Sánchez, Zack Wheeler, a revitalized Aaron Nola, and Jesús Luzardo if they can get him back in time, but at the same time, that wasn't enough against the Mets in the 2024 NLDS or the Dodgers in the 2025 division series a year later. They each countered with shutdown pitching on their side, and hung in there until the Phillies inevitably had to reach into their volatile bullpen to capitalize.
And nothing about the 2026 club suggests that this time would be any different; not when Braves and Dodgers can continue to match them beat for beat talent-wise, while having already proved that they both play much smarter games – in the field, at the plate, and even more so on the base paths – and definitely not after they just showed that they're apparently not that much further above the lowly Mets.
Brandon Marsh, who had an All-Star first half, has one extra-base hit this month.
J.T. Realmuto, once labeled the best catcher in baseball, struck out six times in the Mets series and is a .213 hitter in his mid-30s.
Luis Arráez, who has batted well above .300 for years, suddenly dipped to a .285 average as a Phillie, and while Alec Bohm is impressing with a .328 average through the month, he's never going to hit with the power many hoped for out of a former first-round draft pick at a listed 6'4" and isn't going to suddenly discover it now at age 30 while heading toward free agency.
That leaves Harper and Schwarber as the star sluggers, but at this point, as bats who can be managed around or even directly challenged, while Turner seems to perpetually volley between a $300 million force one minute and a guy who looks like he forgot how to play shortstop the next.
Here's the catch, too: the above names are either in their late 20s at their youngest or pushing well into their 30s on average, after repeated years of trying and failing to out-thump the competition, and with not many more shots expected to be left, especially now that a labor strike puts a serious threat over 2027.
The Phils had a great August, but that was always with a tough September schedule looming, which was always going to tell you what kind of team they really were.
And while there are still six games left, and a probable postseason clinch, there's enough of a picture to tell you this: The Phillies aren't serious.
They haven't been, and really, unless something way more drastic happened at the deadline or Crawford or Painter instantly became the new faces of the franchise, that reality was staring everyone in the face all winter – when the only noticeable difference to the lineup was that Nick Castellanos wasn't in it anymore.
Are they still good enough for October? To get there, sure...probably...hopefully, after this week?
But any further than that? No. They haven't shown anything to say otherwise, or that they're any different from the last two Phillies clubs that hit a hard stop.

item.content:encoded:
This 2026 Twins team makes me sad. The AL Central was more than winnable this year. But here we are, on track for another sub-.500 season. The vibe is much different, however, with top prospects Kaelen Culpepper, Walker Jenkins, and Emmanuel Rodríguez finally with the parent club, looking to guide them toward sustained postseason contention. Actually, yeah, let’s keep talking about the future. I don’t want to talk about the 2026 Twins anymore. Not even fluoxetine helps with my Twins-induced angst. Let’s get into projections!
(Author’s note: Yes, yes, I know. Lockout, and all that. Still, baseball will happen in 2027. As Fred Durst so eloquently said, "You gotta have faith!")
 
Catchers (2): Ryan Jeffers, Victor Caratini
At this point, the consensus is that Minnesota will extend the qualifying offer to Jeffers, which will be around $23 million. Many believe he will decline it and pursue a more lucrative, long-term deal in free agency, which I understand. In fact, it’s what I think Jeffers should do. The Yankees could give him soooooooooooo much money. Still, I wouldn’t be shocked if he accepted the one-year qualifying offer, given the unique predicament players face this offseason.

 
Admittedly, it would be a little anticlimactic for the Twins’ most substantial offseason investment to be a player already on the club. But there are worse things than rostering one of the best-hitting catchers in the sport on what is functionally a one-year, $23-million deal. If Jeffers returns, Caratini will again be his backup, completing the second season of a two-year, $14-million deal he signed last offseason. That’s fine. There are much, much worse tandems in the sport.
 
Hey, at least the Twins aren’t paying J.T. Realmuto $15 million next season, right?! Regardless, one more season of Jeffers as the club’s primary catcher would be an ideal segue to Vahn Lackey taking over as the club’s long-term answer at the position.

 
Infielders (6): Kody Clemens, Xavier Edwards, Brooks Lee, Kaelen Culpepper, Ryan Kreidler, Gabriel González
The Twins can’t march into a 162-game season with Royce Lewis and Kody Clemens penciled in as the primary starters on the right side of the infield and expect to be serious postseason contenders—particularly Lewis. He’s been a below-average hitter for three seasons and is a defensive liability at every infield position, including first base. That being the case, I predict Minnesota will non-tender Lewis, redirecting the roughly $6 million he would have received in arbitration elsewhere.

 
Minnesota could sign a free-agent first baseman (Jake Bauers, Ty France or Luis Arraez?) or trade for a high-ceiling option in St. Louis’s Alec Burleson. However, I’m predicting the club will acquire switch-hitting, speedy, high-OBP second baseman Xavier Edwards from the Miami Marlins to take over the position full-time, while shifting the power-hitting Clemens back down the defensive spectrum.

 
Lee and Culpepper are the most exciting young left side of the infield since Miguel Sanó and Jorge Polanco in the late 2010s. Lee will be the primary third baseman, with Culpepper at short. Despite struggling at the plate, Kreidler is a plus defensive third baseman and shortstop, who will continue to mix in at second and in the outfield. He will also be out of minor-league options next season, giving him the inside edge over fellow utility infielder Ben Ross. González could mix in as a platoon partner with Clemens at first base, starting against left-handed starting pitchers, while also playing occasionally in the corner outfield spots. He'd probably be the 13th position player, seeing very little action and constantly at risk of being demoted to Triple-A St. Paul—unless the Twins wise up and learn how to use their whole bench, instead of just part of it.

 
Outfielders (5): Byron Buxton, Walker Jenkins, Emmanuel Rodríguez, Luke Keaschall, Austin Martin
There has never been a better opportunity to slide Buxton to a corner outfielder/designated hitter role. Both Rodríguez and Jenkins are viable major-league center fielders, with club decision-makers preferring Jenkins over Rodríguez at the position. Both are better defensive center fielders than Buxton at this point in their respective careers. Buxton will be on the other side of hip surgery by then, anyway; his days in the outfield might be numbered.

 
Until (or if) that happens, however, the primary outfield configuration entering next season will probably be Jenkins, Buxton, and Keaschall, with Rodríguez mixing in at all three positions. This level of flexibility permits Twins decision-makers to move on from Trevor Larnach, non-tendering him this offseason. Martin could retain a similar platoon role as this season, starting in either corner outfield spot against left-handed pitching.

 
As with Buxton, I’d prefer Keaschall receiving more DH opportunities, potentially taking over as the club’s primary option there with Josh Bell expected to depart. Being able to keep Keaschall’s bat in the lineup without worrying about defense would be a win-win for the player and the team. He will spend significant time in right field. However, it would be wise to give him and Buxton the majority of DH opportunities, thereby allowing Jenkins and Rodríguez to patrol two-thirds of the outfield almost every game.

 
Starting Rotation (5): Pablo López, Joe Ryan, Taj Bradley, Dean Kremer, Mick Abel
Much was made of the club’s inept bullpen and sluggish second-half offense. Yet, starting rotation woes were quietly the Twins' Achilles’ heel in 2026. So many games were quickly upended by early implosions from Bailey Ober, Zebby Matthews, Connor Prielipp, Mike Paredes, Kendry Rojas, Dean Kremer, and even frontline starters like Joe Ryan and Taj Bradley. Again, bad starts are a part of the sport. Every starter (not named Jacob Misiorowski) has them. Still, starting pitching needs to improve for Minnesota to return to the postseason in 2027.

 
On paper, López, Ryan, and Bradley are a solid top of the rotation. At the same time, however, each could be viewed as an unknown quantity, with López returning from a torn UCL; Ryan undergoing another pronounced late-season fade; and Bradley having what is only his first above-average season as a major-league starter. Still, I'm confident these three can lead what could be a plus rotation.
 
Abel impressed before undergoing arthroscopic surgery on his right elbow in July, and I'm optimistic he could thrive over a full, healthy season, potentially blossoming into a frontline starter. Despite having his worst season in the majors this year, Kremer has been steady since joining the Twins, all but guaranteeing the arb-eligible righty will be a member of Minnesota’s Opening Day 2027 starting rotation. Prielipp will probably be the organization’s sixth starting pitcher who could quickly join the parent club if performance concerns or injuries arise. (That is to say, he'll probably be in the rotation by Opening Day; I'm just not sticking my neck out as to which pitcher is going to get hurt.)
 
Bullpen (8): Jeff Hoffman, Andrew Morris, Joe Jiménez, Yoendrys Gómez, Kody Funderburk, Tommy Nance, Anthony Banda, Zebby Matthews
Beyond Jeffers returning and trading for Edwards, the bullpen is where the majority of Minnesota’s offseason activity could occur. Alternatively, it could look almost identical to how it does now. I’m predicting the latter will happen, with a few substantial shakeups. Twins decision-makers will make a splashy reliever addition this offseason, which I predict will be the club signing Joe Jiménez to a one-year deal. To preface, yes, I know Jiménez hasn’t pitched in the majors since 2024. However, his injury was leg-related, with him undergoing left knee articular cartilage surgery in November 2024. He missed this season with the same injury. However, he is now on a rehab assignment with Atlanta’s Triple-A affiliate, meaning he could be ready to pitch this postseason.

 
When Jiménez last pitched, he was one of the best relievers in baseball. He also has the platonic ideal Twins reliever arsenal, throwing his four-seamer and slider a combined 96% of the time. I think Hoffman will enter next season as the club’s closer, given Gómez’s late-season struggles. Morris should continue operating in a high-leverage role, with the aforementioned Gómez also occupying a late-inning role early next season.
 
Funderburk (out of minor-league options) and Banda could serve as a viable left-handed relief tandem, with Nance working in a mid-leverage role. Also, I project Matthews to earn the eighth and final bullpen spot. However, I expect Minnesota will continue to stretch him out as a starter, with him shuttling between Triple-A and the parent club as ever-important starting-pitching depth. Rojas, Paredes, David Festa, and Ryan Gallagher could occupy a similar role, with Travis Adams, Garrett Acton, Marco Raya, and potential offseason additions as priority Triple-A short-relief depth.

item.content:encoded:
SAN FRANCISCO — First, the good news: outfielder Bo Davidson and infielder Marcelo Mayer will make their long-awaited Giants debuts on Monday night at Oracle Park against the Minnesota Twins. Now, the bad: Bryce Eldridge and Jung Hoo Lee became the latest players to hit the injured list.
Mayer, acquired at the trade deadline from the Boston Red Sox, was reinstated from the injured list, while Davidson was called up from Triple-A Sacramento. Davidson will play right field and bat third in his major-league debut, while Mayer will bat fourth and be the team’s designated hitter.
“Just showing them what I can do and giving them the best I can every game until the season’s over,” Davidson said when asked what he could provide. “Just showing them what Bo is.”
What is Bo?
“You’ll see,” Davidson said with a smile.
Meanwhile, Eldridge landed on the seven-day concussion list after bumping his head at the team’s hotel in Los Angeles, while Lee landed on the 10-day injured list with a groin contusion after fouling a ball off himself on Sunday. Lee’s season is over, and manager Tony Vitello said he doesn’t anticipate Eldridge will play again this season, which ends Sunday.
With Lee landing on the injured list, every member of the Opening Day lineup is either on the injured list (Lee, Willy Adames, Rafael Devers, Matt Chapman, Logan Webb, Casey Schmitt, Harrison Bader) or has been traded (Patrick Bailey, Heliot Ramos, Luis Arraez). The only players from the Opening Day roster still on the roster are infielder Christian Koss and right-hander Landen Roupp.
Adames (left elbow sprain) took grounders and batting practice on Monday afternoon, but he’s very unlikely to return before the end of the season.
Eldridge, who will turn 22 next month, exceeded expectations as a rookie and should be a foundational piece of the Giants’ lineup alongside Devers. Over 107 games, Eldridge hit .269/.364/.461 with 17 home runs, 23 doubles and 57 RBIs. Among rookies, Eldridge’s 130 wRC+ (weighted runs created plus) was the third-highest in the majors.
“Incredibly impressive,” Vitello said of Eldridge’s season. “We summarized that a little bit with him this morning in there. Maturity is the word that gets thrown around a bunch, but it got thrown around in there, too. I think consistency is the other word. He attached that to himself in a good way, not in a braggadocious way.
“If I could speak for him through his own words, a big difference between last year and this year is understanding the ups and downs and how to maintain consistency, which is a lot easier to formulate or plan out than it is to put into act.”
Along with the offense, Vitello also highlighted Eldridge’s defense, which was his biggest question as a prospect. After committing 18 errors in 2024 and 9 in 2025, Eldridge only had two errors this season in the majors and minors. Eldridge also graded out well by Baseball Savant’s new first baseman receiving metric.
Going into next season, one area where Vitello believes Eldridge can improve is baserunning.
“He’s got good instincts, but there’s so many things that he’s seeing for the first time in his life, literally,” Vitello said. “Safety bunts, stuff like that. And then on the base running … he didn’t do anything that would cause us to jump here in the dugout or cost us big, but for a guy that’s going to be on base as often as he is — and he’s not a burner — he’s got to be good on those little separators of reads, preparation before a pitch.”
Davidson, 24, is the Giants’ No. 5 prospect, per Baseball America. Over 125 games this season with Double-A Richmond and Triple-A Sacramento, Davidson hit .290 with 29 home runs, 20 steals and 94 RBIs. He was a candidate to get called up earlier this month but missed a week after fouling a ball off his foot on Sept. 9.
For all of Davidson’s production on the field, he believes the biggest area he’s grown has been “being a better man off the field.”
Davidson is one of many intriguing prospects in a farm system that has climbed the rankings. Along with Davidson, the Giants’ farm system is headlined by shortstops Josuar Gonzalez and Luis Hernandez, as well as right-handed pitcher Jackson Flora.
“We’ve got a very special group of guys that’s coming through,” said Davidson, whose mother, brother, girlfriend and daughter will be in attendance. “The farm itself, the numbers this year just showed. Us being really good brothers off the field, it just shows on the field with the chemistry.”
“I’m excited to see Bo again,” Vitello said. “Just kind of knowing who he was in high school and junior college. … We were able to get him some action in spring training, and then you’re following along, following along. We knew [his promotion] would happen at some point.”
Mayer, 23, was traded to the Giants on Aug. 3 from the Boston Red Sox in exchange for lefty reliever Erik Miller and minor-league outfielder Carlos Gutierrez. The infielder had been recovering from a bone stress reaction to the left ulna, as well as a bone bruise on his right foot.
Vitello anticipates Mayer will primarily be the team’s designated hitter over the final six games, but he could also see some time in the infield.

item.content:encoded:
Twins Video
Box Score:
Starting Pitcher: Dean Kremer: 6 IP, 1 H, 0 ER, 3 BB, 8 K (96 Pitches, 60 Strikes, 62.5%)
Home Runs: Alan Roden (1)
Top 3 WPA: Kremer (0.28), Josh Bell (0.18), Roden (0.13)
Win Probability Chart (Via BaseballSavant):

The Twins are in full "let's see what we have for next year" mode. Sunday found them finishing up a series against a team that is always planning for next year (though rarely making decisions that support that vision): the L.A. Angels.
That meant Walker Jenkins hitting leadoff, the return of Alan Roden, and Ben Ross playing shortstop. Dean Kremer took the mound for the Twins, opposing Ryan Johnson—who, like many Angels pitchers, has had an encouraging second half.
The Twins had a hard time squaring up Johnson, who has a funky, quick delivery with lots of side-to-side movement. There was a lot of weak contact on the ground until the third inning, when with one out, Jenkins legged out an infield single and Brooks Lee followed with a hard single to right. Josh Bell looped in a single to score Jenkins, and Roden delivered yet another single to score Lee. That made it 2-0 Twins.
Kremer wasn't at his sharpest early, with his velocity down a bit and looking a little off in terms of command. But he bore down when he had to, getting the light-hitting Angels to chase and taking advantage of the fact they burned all their challenges by the second inning. They didn't collect their first hit until the fourth, when Vaughn Grissom singled, but he was quickly erased on a double-play grounder from catcher Moisés Ballesteros.
Lee and Bell peppered Johnson with a couple more singles in the fifth, resulting in another RBI for Bell and chasing Johnson from the game. Kremer found his rhythm as the outing progressed, still staying out of the middle of the zone but throwing a few more strikes. He managed eight strikeouts through six innings, with a lot of whiffs on his four-seamer, despite touching 94 MPH just once.
The top of the sixth was very on brand for the Angels. With two outs, Emmanuel Rodríguez doubled off Jose Siri's glove. It was a play that would have been lauded as really nice had Siri made the catch, but in reality, he had plenty of time and barely had to jump. Regardless, Rodríguez deserved the break; he has really struggled lately. Ross singled him home, then tried to steal second. For some reason, Ross decided not to slide, which turned from a poor to a perfect choice when the ball scooted into center field. He coasted into third, then realized the Angels were picking up the ball with little urgency, turned on the jets, and scored.
The valiant visitors would add on in the seventh. Lee and Bell produced their third hits of the game, both singles. Roden then pulverized a first-pitch slider from lefty Sammy Peralta for a three-run homer. It's notable that Roden looked overmatched against Peralta in the fifth, eventually grounding out weakly, which shows a good ability to adjust on the fly.
Bailey Ober was brought out for the seventh, with the Twins juggling their starting rotation for the last week of the year. He hit 91 MPH and carved up the Angels lineup for the final three innings, allowing only a single (that was really a misplay by Ross at shortstop).
Stuff I'm Tracking:
- I'm going to miss the old version of the Angels, who were always all-in on the current season but made terrible baseball ops decisions, had a terrible culture, and apparently didn't even utilize pitch-tracking data until they revamped their pitching department this August. You just knew trading with them was playing chess while (former owner) Arte Moreno insisted his club play checkers. I still wouldn't have traded Kaelen Culpepper (plus more, reportedly) for Zach Neto, though.
- Royce Lewis looks cooked. No idea what the plan is for him next year. He did loop in a meaningless single in the seventh after striking out swinging his first three at-bats.
- Roden quietly has a .278/.349/.375 slash despite inconsistent playing time, this being his first game since August 26. You do root for a guy like him who hasn't done anything wrong; he's just been a victim of poor roster construction with all the left-handed outfielders on this team who need at-bats.
- Rodríguez is in the meat grinder, constantly behind in counts, and when he swings early, it's in play and an easy out. He did break an 0-17 with the double off Siri's glove in center.
- Is there a better pitcher in the league with a big lead than Ober? When he doesn't have to be perfect (and when he doesn't have to pace himself toward six innings), he looks great.
What’s Next: The Twins head to San Francisco to take on the floundering Giants. Ober was the scheduled starter, but with him pitching in relief, it may be Zebby Matthews taking the turn. Whoever it is will face Landen Roupp (9-14, 4.01 ERA), a solid but unspectacular righty who will be making his 30th start of the year. The Giants have been beset by injuries, and Luis Arraez is still second on the team in bWAR even though he was traded at the deadline. Crazy how a team that thought of itself as a contender is this bereft of talent, despite Rafael Devers quietly having his best overall year. (He's out for the rest of the year with a core muscle injury, leaving the Giants' own core rather damaged.)

item.content:encoded:
Cristopher Sánchez consigue su 18ma victoria, líder de MLB; Juan Soto se va de 4-1
El dominicano Cristopher Sánchez consiguió su 18.ª victoria, la mayor cantidad en las Grandes Ligas, para guiar la victoria el domingo 7-2 de los Filis de Filadelfia ante los Mets de Nueva York.
Los Filis (86-70), que rescataron un empate en la serie de cuatro juegos, llegaron al domingo en el tercer puesto de comodín de la Liga Nacional, a un juego de los Cachorros de Chicago y Padres de San Diego y con una ventaja de cuatro juegos sobre los Diamondbacks de Arizona.
Sánchez permitió seis hits —incluido el jonrón de Bo Bichette en la sexta entrada— y ponchó a seis en 6 1/3 innings, con lo que rompió el empate con Sonny Gray, de los Medias Rojas de Boston, por el liderato de victorias en las Grandes Ligas.
El último lanzador de los Filis en liderar las mayores en victorias fue Steve Carlton, con 23 en 1982.
Justin Crawford conectó un triple de tres carreras y el venezolano Luis Arráez terminó con dos carreras impulsadas. Alec Bohm y Trea Turner aportaron cada uno un hit productor. Kyle Schwarber igualó su máximo de carrera con cuatro bases por bolas.
El novato Jonah Tong (2-2) permitió cuatro carreras y ponchó a cinco en 4 2/3 innings por los coleros Mets, que terminaron 36-45 en casa —su peor registro en Citi Field desde 2013, que fue de 33-48.
Los Mets atrajeron a 2.712.120 aficionados esta temporada, una caída de 5.870 aficionados por juego respecto a la temporada pasada —el descenso más pronunciado en las Grandes Ligas.
El dominicano Juan Soto bateó de 4-1.

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK (AP) — Cristopher Sánchez earned his major league-leading 18th win Sunday, leading the Philadelphia Phillies to a 7-2 victory over the New York Mets.
The Phillies (86-70), who salvaged a split of the four-game series, entered Sunday in the third National League wild-card spot, one game behind the Chicago Cubs and San Diego Padres and four games clear of the Arizona Diamondbacks.
Sánchez surrendered six hits — including Bo Bichette’s sixth-inning homer — and struck out six over 6 1/3 innings as he snapped a tie with the Boston Red Sox’s Sonny Gray for the big league lead in wins.

Already have an account? Log in to continue.
Otherwise, follow the link below to join.
| Please log in to continue |
The last Phillies pitcher to lead the majors in wins was Steve Carlton with 23 in 1982.
Justin Crawford had a three-run triple and Luis Arraez finished with two RBIs. Alec Bohm and Trea Turner each had run-scoring hits. Kyle Schwarber tied a career high with four walks.
Rookie Jonah Tong (2-2) gave up four runs and struck out five in 4 2/3 innings for the last-place Mets, who finished 36-45 at home — their worst record at Citi Field since the 2013 team went 33-48.
PIRATES 4, ROYALS 3
PITTSBURGH (AP) — Rafael Flores Jr. hit the go-ahead two-run home run in the eighth inning to help Pittsburgh to a win over Kansas City and complete a series sweep.
After Ryan O’Hearn led off with a single to center, Flores sent a slider from Nate Pearson (2-3) into the left-field bleachers for his 10th homer this season.
Pittsburgh rallied with a two-run homer in the eighth for a second straight day. Brandon Lowe had his 33rd of the season in a 6-5 win Saturday.
Carmen Mlodzinki (8-7) got the win. He allowed two runs and three hits in three innings. The reliever gave up a pinch-hit, two-run home run to Vinnie Pasquantino that gave Kansas City a 3-2 lead with two outs in the seventh.
Mason Montgomery earned his 16th save. He retired the first two batters in the ninth before Luke Maile hit a double and took third on a fielding error by Jake Mangum. Montgomery got Isaac Collins to fly out to right to strand Maile.
The Royals went ahead 1-0 in the first inning with three straight singles off Lake Bachar. Bobby Witt Jr. beat out a groundball to second baseman Lowe. He moved to third on a single to right from Jac Caglianone and scored when Perez shot one through the middle of the infield.
RAYS 5, RED SOX 1
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — Griffin Jax tossed five shutout innings and the Tampa Bay crept closer to the AL East title with a victory over Boston.
The Rays will have an opportunity to clinch the franchise’s fifth division title during Tuesday’s doubleheader at the New York Yankees.
Boston would have clinched a playoff spot with a victory. The Red Sox, who were 32-46 and 15 1/2 games back in the AL East on June 24, have since gone 52-25. They could still wrap up a spot Sunday with a Houston loss.
Jax (8-10) allowed three singles and worked out of a bases-loaded jam in the fifth inning by striking out Roman Anthony. Cole Sulser, Brody Hopkins and Steven Matz each pitched an inning of scoreless relief.
Boston’s Trevor Story spoiled the shutout in the ninth with a one-out home run off right-hander Ty Johnson.
The Rays scored four first-inning runs off left-hander Patrick Sandoval (1-7). Jonny DeLuca smashed a two-run, bases-loaded double down the left-field line and Chandler Simpson followed with a two-run single. Sandoval began the inning by walking Yandy Diaz and Ryan Vilade, then surrendering a single to Junior Caminero.
CUBS 9, REDS 1
CINCINNATI (AP) — Pete Crow-Armstrong hit his 45th home run as Chicago moved closer to clinching a postseason berth with a victory over Cincinnati.
Chicago (87-69) reduced its magic number to one and could wrap up a berth if the Diamondbacks lose to the Yankees later Sunday.
The Cubs began the day tied with the Padres and one game ahead of the Phillies for the top NL wild-card spot which would earn them home-field advantage in the wild-card round. The Cubs own the tiebreakers over the Diamondbacks, Padres, and Phillies.
Cubs third baseman Alex Bregman left Sunday’s game in the fourth inning after being struck in the face by a foul ball off the bat of Michael Busch while standing near the on-deck circle.
Cubs left-hander David Peterson (9-8) allowed a run on three hits in seven innings with one walk and seven strikeouts.
The Cubs loaded the bases with one out in the third. Ian Happ singled in a run and Nico Hoerner walked to force in another to extend Chicago’s lead to 3-0. Pedro Ramirez’s two-run single made the score 5-0.
Reds right-hander Rhett Lowder (6-12) allowed five earned runs on six hits with three walks and three strikeouts.
CARDINALS 5, NATIONALS 3
ST. LOUIS (AP) — Iván Herrera hit a pair of home runs, and Leo Bernal also homered as St. Louis scored three runs in the eighth inning to come from behind and beat Washington.
Bernal hit his fifth homer of the season off Yovanny Cruz (0-2) after Erik Tolman walked Jordan Walker with two outs in the eighth inning.
Herrera hit his second homer of the game and 18th of the season to tie the game at 3-all after hitting a solo shot in the first inning.
It was Herrera’s third career multi-homer game and second this season after going deep twice on June 13 at Minnesota.
Luis Gastelum (5-3) pitched a scoreless eighth inning for St. Louis, and Riley O’Brien pitched a perfect ninth to earn his National League-leading 38th save.
Cardinals starter Quinn Mathews allowed three runs on seven hits and two walks in a career-high seven innings.
Jake Irvin allowed two runs on three hits and had eight strikeouts in 5 1/3 innings for the Nationals.

item.content:encoded:
The Mets (70-84) defeated the Philadelphia Phillies (85-69) by a score of 6-3.
Here are the takeaways...
-- Mets left-handed starter Zac Thornton plunked leadoff batter Kyle Schwarber on a 3-2 count to get the game started. The rookie battled back, striking out Trea Turner and Bryce Harper before Mets first baseman Brett Baty made a diving stop on a Luis Arraez grounder down the line to put away the third out.
-- Southpaw Tim Mayza served as the bullpen opener for Philadelphia, and Francisco Lindor jumped all over him with a leadoff double. With one out, Bo Bichette worked a 10-pitch at-bat, culminating in a single to center field which moved Lindor up to third base. Carson Benge kept the line moving and drove in Lindor with an opposite-field single. Mark Vientos was walked to load the bases, and Phillies manager Don Mattingly pulled Mayza for right-handed reliever Jose Urquidy. A.J. Ewing roped an Urquidy fastball for a double, which scored two runs. Urquidy retired the next two Mets batters to limit the damage to three runs.
-- In the second inning, Ewing got turned around on a deep line drive to center, failing to haul in the RBI double for Bryson Stott, which cut the Mets' lead to 3-1. In the bottom half of the inning, Juan Soto doubled into the left-center field gap with two outs, but Urquidy struck out Bichette to end the threat.
-- With two outs away in the top of the sixth, Phillies left fielder Edmundo Sosa blasted a solo shot to left field, his third hit of the night. Excluding Sosa, Thornton allowed just two hits. He struck out four and walked one, allowing two earned runs across 87 pitches.
-- Soto took a hanging breaking ball thrown by Phillies right-hander Orion Kerkering 428 feet for a two-out three-run homer in the bottom of the sixth. Soto's 26th tater of 2026 put the Mets up 6-2.
-- Philadelphia center fielder Derek Hill responded with a solo home run off of Mets left-handed reliever Nate Lavender in the top of the seventh. Lavender persevered, retiring each of the next four batters he faced, before handing the ball to Dedniel Núñez to record the third out of the eighth. In the bottom half of the frame, Bichette grounded into a double play with the bases loaded. Núñez handled the ninth inning and retired the side to earn the first save of his season - and second save of his career - to seal the 6-3 win for the Mets.
Game MVP: Juan Soto
Soto notched his third game with multiple extra-base hits in September, going 3-for-5 with a double and a three-run homer. It was also Soto's third game of the season with at least three hits.
Highlights
What's next
The Mets play the Phillies in the third game of the four-game home series on Saturday at 4:10 p.m. on SNY. They will honor 2026 Baseball Hall of Fame inductee Carlos Beltrán.
New York will send out Christian Scott (3.76 ERA, 1.26 WHIP in 105.1 IP).
Philadelphia is set to start fellow right-hander Andrew Painter (5.54 ERA, 1.44 WHIP in 115.1 IP).

item.content:encoded:
PITTSBURGH — Nick Gonzales has been one of the Pittsburgh Pirates' best hitters, and he could finish as one of the best in baseball.
Gonzales has hit .304/.367/.392 for an OPS of .759 in 141 games for the Pirates, giving him the best batting average and the fourth-best in the National League, with nine games left in the 2026 season.
The Pirates have Gonzales starting at third base in the series opener against the Kansas City Royals at PNC Park on Sept. 18, and it's another chance for him to finish his season strong.
Gonzales also has a realistic chance of winning the NL Batting Title, with Freddy Sanchez the last Pirates player to do so in 2006, batting .344.
Who Gonzales Faces in the NL Batting Title
NL Batting Title Leaders
| Player | Batting Average | Team |
|---|---|---|
| Luis Arraez | .315 | Philadelphia Phillies |
| Gabriel Moreno | .307 | Arizona Diamondbacks |
| Otto Lopez | .306 | Miami Marlins |
| Nick Gonzales | .304 | Pittsburgh Pirates |
| TJ Rumfield | .301 | Colorado Rockies |
Gonzales ranks fourth in the NL and is nine points behind Philadelphia Phillies second baseman Luis Arraez, who leads with a .315 batting average.
Arraez is always towards the top of the batting average leaderboards, winning three straight batting titles from 2022 to 2024, .316 with the Minnesota Twins in 2022, .354 with the Miami Marlins in 2023 and then .314 with both the Marlins and the Padres in 2024.
Moreno is having a career year, like Gonzales, and has never hit above .300 before. He's been excellent in September, batting .333/.410/.611 for a 1.021 OPS.
Lopez is also putting up his best season yet, and has bounced back from a poor August by hitting .316/.418/.404 for an OPS of .822 in September.
Rumfield has been great in his rookie season and at his very best this month, batting .408/.491/.633 for an OPS of 1.124.
Why Gonzales Winning Batting Title Means to Pirates
Gonzales has been a constant for the Pirates on the basepaths and someone they can rely on to get a rally going.
He hit his best in July, .388/.438/.544 for an OPS of .982, but has hit just .260/.352/.323 for an OPS of .675 since the start of August.
Gonzales needs to put up some great numbers to overtake Arraez and the other competition, but it's not impossible.
He's gotten more time at designated hitter than at third base, with his defensive struggles, but he's absolutely been an important part of the Pirates' offense.
"I hope he gets there and I hope he does it," Pirates manager Don Kelly said about Gonzales. "Awesome for him to be in the top of the batting order in the National League, and I hope that he can get up there and win it. He should take pride in that in how he's been able to swing the bat for us. He's had some huge at-bats, and swung the bat well and been a big part of our offensive success this year."
Dominic writes for Pittsburgh Pirates On SI, Pittsburgh Panthers Pn SI and also, Pittsburgh Steelers On SI. A Pittsburgh native, Dominic grew up watching Pittsburgh Sports and wrote for The Pitt News as an undergraduate at the University of Pittsburgh, covering Pitt Athletics. He would write for Pittsburgh Sports Now after college and has years of experience covering sports across Pittsburgh.
